output.title: Early signs your AI workflow is drifting
output.body:
Eval drift is not a theory problem for a small business; it is a workflow problem. In plain English, it means an AI-assisted process slowly starts giving answers that are less consistent, less useful, or just confidently wrong for your use case. If that process touches customer replies, approvals, or order handling, drift becomes an operational risk, not a model debate.

The first question is simple: do you already have one repetitive, high-frequency workflow where AI filters, ranks, or responds to inputs, and would problems show up as customer complaints, missed approvals, failed orders, or manual rework? If the answer is no, there is nothing to monitor yet. If the answer is yes, pick one control and write it down.

A practical first control is a monthly manual spot-check against a small set of past cases, using the original success criteria. Keep it human-readable: what came in, what the system output, and whether a person would still sign off on it. Any threshold is your own operating rule, not a Bareni benchmark.

In a free 30-minute diagnostic, the useful question is: “Is eval drift a real risk in this workflow, or are we trying to solve a problem we do not have yet?” That keeps the decision bounded. If drift monitoring belongs anywhere, it belongs inside a pilot scope with human approval before any retraining or policy change. Small business automation works better when it fails politely, not mysteriously.
